h1: New York to Texas car shipping
heroSub: Texas is the second most common out-of-state move we book from New York. Here is what the run costs to each major city, which highways the trucks use, and what Texas expects of you once the car arrives.
intro:
New York to Texas car shipping covers 1,550 to 1,800 miles, depending on whether the car is headed to Dallas, Houston, Austin, San Antonio or farther west. A running sedan on an open carrier typically costs $1,000 to $1,100 from the NYC metro and arrives 4 to 6 days after pickup. Trucks run both directions all year, which keeps pricing steady.

Our Bronx, Yonkers, Hempstead and Babylon offices load Texas-bound cars several times a week, and the Albany and Buffalo offices feed the same trucks. The quote tool beside the heading gives a live price; the figures here are typical ranges.

sections.h2: The two highway paths used for New York to Texas car shipping
sections.html:
The dispatcher picks the path based on the delivery city. For Dallas, Fort Worth, Austin and most of North and Central Texas, trucks leave the metro on I-78, drop down I-81 through the Shenandoah Valley, pick up I-40 at Knoxville and run through Nashville and Memphis before turning south on I-30 at Little Rock into Dallas. That is about 1,550 miles and the most direct line.

For Houston and the Gulf coast, many carriers prefer I-95 to the Carolinas, I-85 through Atlanta, then I-20 across Alabama and Mississippi to Shreveport and down into Houston, closer to 1,650 miles. San Antonio can go either way. El Paso sits 1,800 miles out on I-20 and I-10, closer to Phoenix than to Houston.

sections.h2: What New York to Texas car shipping costs by destination
sections.html:
The typical open-carrier price for a running mid-size sedan from the NYC metro to Dallas, Houston, Austin or San Antonio is $1,000 to $1,100 booked about a week out. Enclosed adds 30 to 50 percent, so figure $1,350 to $1,600. El Paso adds about $150 because fewer trucks finish their run there. Lubbock, Midland and Odessa in the oil patch are similar: trucks do not pass through naturally, so the dispatcher pays for a detour.

Pickup trucks deserve their own line because Texas is where they go. An F-150 or Silverado 1500 adds $100 to $150 over a sedan; a crew-cab three-quarter-ton or a lifted truck can add $200 to $250 and may need a carrier with the deck height for it. The car shipping cost guide lists every surcharge. Summer is the busy season, and the weeks around Thanksgiving and Christmas tighten up too.

sections.h2: Who is moving from New York to Texas and where they land
sections.html:
Most cars on this lane belong to people relocating. Finance firms have moved teams to Dallas and the Uptown and Plano office corridors. Tech hiring pulls people to Austin and Round Rock. Energy, medicine and the port pull people to Houston, from the Energy Corridor out to The Woodlands. The absence of a state income tax comes up constantly, and it has made Texas the busiest corporate relocation destination we serve after Florida.

Military orders are the second big group: Fort Cavazos (still Fort Hood to most people) at Killeen, Fort Bliss at El Paso, Joint Base San Antonio, and Fort Sam Houston. Our military car shipping page covers gate access and PCS timing. Students round it out in August and January: UT Austin, Texas A&M, Rice and UNT. College Station is an hour off the truck path, so allow a day of flexibility.

sections.h2: Delivering across a state the size of Texas
sections.html:
Texas is 800 miles across, and a driver who delivers in Dallas on Tuesday is not going to be in El Paso on Wednesday. Dallas–Fort Worth is the easiest delivery metro in the state, with wide suburban streets and a dense carrier network; Plano, Frisco and Arlington get daily service. Houston is almost as easy, though Montrose and the Heights have tight streets, so the driver may ask to meet at a nearby lot. Austin's downtown and the hills west of MoPac are tight for a full hauler.

El Paso and the Rio Grande Valley around McAllen are each a full day beyond the main metros. Trucks run there less often, so a pickup window of a week is realistic. Lubbock and Midland get oil-field traffic, but expect price and transit at the top of the range. For a small town, the driver will often ask to meet at the nearest highway exit; the door-to-door page explains that handoff.

sections.h2: Toll tags, E-ZPass and registering the car in Texas
sections.html:
Before pickup, take the E-ZPass transponder out of the windshield and keep it with you. Texas toll roads in Dallas, Houston and Austin read E-ZPass tags through interoperability agreements, and a hauler crossing a dozen gantries with your tag in the window can bill your account for every one. Once settled, a TxTag, TollTag or EZ TAG is what locals use, and all three work statewide.

Texas gives new residents 30 days to register the vehicle. The county tax office will want proof of Texas insurance, the title or lender information, and an inspection where it still applies. The state has been changing its inspection rules, so check the TxDMV site the week you arrive.

sections.h2: Heat, hurricanes and what to check before the car loads
sections.html:
From June through September the delivery yard is often over 100 degrees and the car has been on an open deck in that sun for days. A weak battery that started fine in Yonkers may not turn over in Houston. Check the battery, top up coolant and oil, and leave about a quarter tank; a full tank adds weight and expands in the heat.

Hurricane season on the Gulf coast runs June through November and peaks in August and September. When a storm is in the Gulf, carriers stop taking Houston deliveries two or three days out and hold cars at Dallas or San Antonio until roads clear. That is a delay, not a loss; the car is safer inland on a truck than in a Houston driveway during a storm surge. Keep your dates flexible and run the pre-shipping checklist so the car is ready to sit a few extra days.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to ship a car from New York to Texas?
faqs.a: A running mid-size sedan on an open carrier typically costs $1,000 to $1,100 from the New York metro to Dallas, Houston, Austin or San Antonio. Enclosed transport runs $1,350 to $1,600. El Paso, the Valley and West Texas add roughly $150. Pickups and SUVs add $100 to $250, and summer or holiday weeks push prices toward the top of the range.

faqs.q: How long does New York to Texas car shipping take?
faqs.a: Most deliveries land 4 to 6 days after pickup. Dallas is fastest at 4 to 5 days because it sits at the end of the I-40 and I-30 line. Houston and Austin are 4 to 6. El Paso, Lubbock and the Rio Grande Valley are 5 to 7 days, since a truck makes a dedicated run past the main metros.

faqs.q: Should I leave my E-ZPass in the car?
faqs.a: No. Remove the transponder from the windshield and take it with you. Texas toll gantries in Dallas, Houston and Austin can read E-ZPass tags through network agreements, and a car hauler crosses a lot of them, so you would be billed for the truck's tolls. Once in Texas, pick up a TxTag, TollTag or EZ TAG.

faqs.q: How soon do I have to register the car in Texas?
faqs.a: Texas gives new residents 30 days to register. You will need Texas insurance, an inspection where it still applies, and the title or lender information. The state has been changing its inspection requirements, so check the TxDMV site the week you arrive. The car ships with its New York plates on; nothing about transport changes the deadline.

faqs.q: What happens if a hurricane hits Houston while my car is in transit?
faqs.a: Carriers stop delivering to the Gulf coast two or three days before a storm and hold vehicles inland, usually at a yard in Dallas or San Antonio, until roads reopen. Your car stays with the truck rather than being dropped in a flood zone. Expect a delay of several days and a call from us with a new delivery window.
